title: Remember.
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later diagrams reviewed. Begin after the final illustrated Rb7+ near 177 seconds: White Kb8/Rb7/b4/d3 against Kb6/Bc6/Qg1/Rh1/b5/d4/g3/g2, Black to move. Native58 shows the complete board before the rook move, native59 its b7 destination highlight while the rook is animating, and native60 confirms Bxb7 and the resulting stalemate. The promoted queen on g1 has already captured the knight; no knight remains. This focused defensive study has one guided stalemate line. Exact draw certificates prove a non-loss for both sides: Black chooses Bxb7; if Black instead chooses Ka6, White uses Ra7+/Kb6/Rb7+ and can claim an actual threefold repetition if Black keeps declining. Every opposing reply and the repetition’s legal move history are saved and checked; an isolated FEN or narrated perpetual-check assertion is insufficient. Earlier Ng1, d3, rook waiting moves and promotion choices remain outside this selected proof.
transcript: There are some chess positions that are meant to remind us why we fell in love with this game. In this position, it seems like white is completely lost. The material is equal, except that black has three extra pawns that are very close to promoting. After anything that white does, black is going to have this move rook to F1, stopping the check of the white rook trying to attack the black king. And if the rook shuffles to E2 trying to come here, now the bishop stops the check and white is going to be left with no good moves. Black is simply going to get a queen and win the game. But white has an incredible resource in this position, starting with the brilliant knight to G1. Now, this is a real threat. If the knight is captured, rook F6 is going to be checkmate, meaning that the knight is untouchable and black has to spend a move to play king to B6. To follow up, rook to F6 with bishop to C6. This fearless soldier is defending his king. And again, white is left with no hope. But the player with the white pieces knows that hope dies last, and he plays the only drawing move in this position, the incredible D3. A move that doesn't seem to change anything in the position, but that passes the turn to black. Black ignores this meaningless plan and pushes H2, having now two pawns only one step away from getting a new queen. But white has an ace up his sleeve with the mysterious rook to F7. Now, it seems like black can finally simply get a queen. Has white forgotten about his original plan? Well, no, because rook to F7 prepared the two brilliant rook B7 check. The king, of course, cannot take, and if the bishop takes, this is now a stalemate. None of the white pieces can move, but the white king is not checkmated, meaning that this is a draw. And if the king moves away, well, now we keep checking it and we push it back to where it belongs to then sacrifice the rook one more time. But black is not that naive and he realizes that if he pushes this pawn, now rook to B7 doesn't work. He can simply take the rook because now white can move this knight and now this is not a stalemate. So, white doesn't have rook to B7 anymore and he has to find another only move that saves this position, the brilliant rook H7. If black ever tries to move the bishop, we can simply go back to checking the king and the only move for black is to bring the bishop back. And the same happens if this king moves. We go back here and we're threatening checkmate in one move, forcing black to come back to defend the bishop. But this would have not worked, for example, with rook to G7 because now black can play bishop to E8, defending the checking square and now winning the game. So, after this brilliant move, black can only push the pawn and white is going to shuffle between these two squares. And finally, this is going to be a beautiful zugzwang. Black has no other choice but to take this knight, allowing rook to B7 and a draw for white.
